title: From a model call to a configurable chatbot
summary: How the LangChain chatbot combines MongoDB conversation memory, optional Presidio anonymization, provider configuration and LangSmith tracing, with the trade-offs and the parts that are still open.
lead: A model API can return an answer in a few lines of code. A reusable chatbot needs more decisions: how to keep a conversation, how to configure behavior, which provider to call, what to store, and how to debug a bad answer. In this post I walk through my langchain-chatbot repository, where I turned those decisions into an application with MongoDB memory, optional Presidio anonymization, provider configuration and LangSmith tracing. I cover the design choices, the request path, how to run it, and what is still limited or unfinished.

sections.title: The problem: more than a model call
paragraphs: Calling a hosted model is the easy part of a chatbot. The work starts when the second message arrives. The bot has to remember the first one, so history must be stored somewhere and loaded for the right conversation. Its tone and instructions should be adjustable without editing code. The provider should be a configuration choice, not a rewrite. And when an answer is wrong, there has to be a way to see which prompt and which intermediate values produced it.

My langchain-chatbot project is my attempt to put those concerns into one running application. According to my README, the base model is Vertex AI or the OpenAI API, memory is MongoDB, the interface is a Next.js frontend with a FastAPI backend, and prompt versioning and tracing go through LangSmith. Users can shape the bot's personality by setting attributes such as gender and age. I added one more concern on top: personal data in user messages can be anonymized before the text reaches the model provider, and mapped back afterwards.

I built the streaming chatbot with MongoDB-backed memory and configurable behavior, added LangSmith prompt versioning and tracing, and integrated Microsoft Presidio for anonymization. I describe the code as it exists in the repository, including parts that are optional or incomplete. I make no claims about throughput, answer quality or cost, because I did not measure them.

sections.title: Separate the interface from orchestration
paragraphs: I started with a chat session in a Gradio interface. My changelog records that history: v1.0 chatted through a Gradio UI and saved conversation memory in MongoDB, and v1.0.1 added streaming responses, collection of user information, and an agent with basic tools. The repository now describes a Next.js frontend and a FastAPI backend, which is the shape this post follows.

I split them for practical reasons. In a UI callback, transport, prompt assembly, model invocation and output handling blur together, and an empty answer could come from any of them. With a backend that owns configuration and orchestration, I can check each layer on its own. Model integration, memory and anonymization are separate components that the backend wires together, so changing a provider or a prompt does not touch the interface code.
My README names the backend components. I summarize them below; the Bot Manager is the class in bot.py that the rest of this post focuses on.

sections.title: Follow one request end to end
paragraphs: My README documents the data flow in four stages. The user sends a message through the frontend, which forwards it to the backend. The backend optionally anonymizes personal data, builds the LangChain conversation chain and calls the selected provider, while LangSmith traces the run. The conversation is stored in MongoDB. If protection is enabled, the model response is de-anonymized before the backend returns it and the frontend renders it.

The order matters: I load history first, because anonymization has to cover the history as well as the new message. Otherwise a name replaced in one turn could reappear in plain text in the next prompt.

definitions.text: A runnable named LoadHistory collects the input, the agent scratchpad and the stored history for the conversation id.
When enabled, the input, history and scratchpad are passed through the Presidio anonymizer before the model sees them.
The chain built by the chain manager runs against the configured provider. The agent executor is limited to three iterations and handles parsing errors.
The reversible anonymizer maps substituted values in the output back to the originals.

code.title: backend/bot.py (abridged)
code.code:
history_loader = RunnableMap({
    "input": itemgetter("input"),
    "agent_scratchpad": itemgetter("intermediate_steps") | RunnableLambda(format_log_to_str),
    "history": itemgetter("conversation_id") | RunnableLambda(self.memory.load_history)
}).with_config(run_name="LoadHistory")

if self.config.enable_anonymizer:
    anonymizer_runnable = self.anonymizer.get_runnable_anonymizer().with_config(run_name="AnonymizeSentence")
    de_anonymizer = RunnableLambda(self.anonymizer.anonymizer.deanonymize).with_config(
        run_name="DeAnonymizeResponse")

    agent = (history_loader
             | anonymizer_runnable
             | self.chain.chain
             | de_anonymizer
             | ReActSingleInputOutputParser())
else:
    agent = history_loader | self.chain.chain | ReActSingleInputOutputParser()

sections.title: Scope memory to the conversation
paragraphs: Memory is the most consequential piece of state in the project, so I want to be specific about how it is keyed. The repository has more than one memory implementation. One wraps LangChain's MongoDB chat message history and is configured with a connection string, database, collection and session identifier. A custom adapter uses pymongo directly: it stores one document per message turn with a conversation id, a session id and the serialized turn, indexes the session id, and loads or deletes history by filtering on both identifiers.

The point of the filter is that history loads for the intended conversation, not for whichever request last touched a shared variable. The base memory class also keeps an in-process dictionary of histories keyed by conversation id, and a window of the last five messages is the default context size. So storing history is separate from choosing what goes into a prompt, and the window is a configuration value rather than a property of the database.

Persistent history brings obligations that code alone does not settle. Retention, deletion and access isolation are policy decisions. My v1.0 changelog is candid about the early state: it lists multi-user handling and saving history with a user id as pending. I would verify both for any deployment rather than assume them.

sections.title: Put PII handling at the provider boundary
paragraphs: Chat messages often contain names, phone numbers and identifiers. If the model provider is a third party, the cleanest place to intervene is the boundary just before the call. I wrapped LangChain's PresidioReversibleAnonymizer as an optional layer. It detects the language of the input (Vietnamese or English, defaulting to English when detection fails or the language is unsupported), then anonymizes the user input, the conversation history and the agent scratchpad. After the model responds, the reversible anonymizer maps the substituted values back, so the user sees a natural answer while the provider never receives the original value.

Making the layer reversible was my main design choice. Plain redaction would remove information the conversation needs: if the user says a phone number and later refers to it, a placeholder token has to stay consistent across turns. Realistic substitutes keep the prompt readable to the model, at the cost of holding a mapping in the backend that I have to handle with care.

The boundary is configuration and data flow, not a guarantee. An anonymizer does not detect every sensitive span, and it helps only where it is switched on. My README and .env.example list it as optional, and the example file sets ENABLE_ANONYMIZER to false. Raw history in MongoDB, trace contents and model input can each follow a different path, so each needs inspection. The recognizers I added in constants.py are a list of US-oriented entity types (bank number, driver license, ITIN, passport, SSN); the repository does not demonstrate coverage of Vietnamese-specific identifiers.

sections.title: What the traces show
paragraphs: The LangSmith traces below come from a Vietnamese conversation I ran in which the user gives a phone number. The first screenshot shows the anonymize step: the real number goes in and a different number comes out. The second shows the model call, where both the user message and the reply contain only the substitute. The third shows the de-anonymize step restoring the original number in the reply.

Seeing the substitution in a trace convinced me more than reading the code, but it is a single example. It shows that the path works for one phone number in one conversation. It is not an evaluation of detection recall, and I redacted the screenshots before publishing.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Traces are a data path too. A tracing setup should show enough structure to debug a failure without assuming that every user message is safe to keep in a third-party dashboard.

sections.title: Use configuration and tracing to iterate
paragraphs: I made bot behavior configurable at several levels. The constructor of the Bot class accepts a prompt template, a memory type, a cache type, a model type, model keyword arguments, a personality string and a list of tools. The default prompt templates are referenced by LangSmith hub names in constants.py, which is where prompt versioning enters the picture: the prompt is identified by name rather than embedded in the Python source. The model types are OpenAI, Vertex AI and llama.cpp, selected through an enum that maps to LangChain model classes.

I enable LangSmith tracing through environment variables, and the Bot waits for tracers to finish after each call so that a run is pushed before the process moves on. I set run names such as LoadHistory, AnonymizeSentence and DeAnonymizeResponse explicitly in the chain, which is why the traces above are easy to read. Naming the steps is a small change that pays for itself the first time a bad answer has to be traced back to a stage.
The default sampling parameters in bot.py use a temperature of 0.2. I have not compared settings against each other, so I do not claim they beat alternatives; they are starting values.

sections.title: Run it with Docker Compose
paragraphs: The repository ships a Compose file for the frontend, backend and database, plus a setup.sh script (setup.bat on Windows) and Makefile targets. My README asks for Python 3.9 or later and Docker with Docker Compose. Compose starts the services in dependency order: the backend waits for a healthy MongoDB and the frontend waits for a healthy backend. The backend health check calls its /health route.

The manual path follows my README. After the services are up, the frontend is on port 3000, the backend on 8080 and the API documentation on /docs. The Compose file publishes MongoDB on host port 27018, mapped to 27017 inside the container; my README diagram shows 27017, so treat the Compose file as the reference.

code.code:
services:
  mongodb:
    image: mongo:latest
    ports:
      - "27018:27017"
  backend:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    depends_on:
      mongodb:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      - backend/.env
    environment:
      - MONGO_URI=mongodb://mongodb:27017/chatbot
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
  frontend:
    build:
      context: ./frontend
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=http://backend:8080
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Running the backend without Docker needs the spaCy models used by the anonymizer, for example python -m spacy download en_core_web_md, plus a MongoDB instance and Node.js for the frontend. Docker does not make the anonymizer on by default; that is controlled by configuration.

sections.title: Limits and trade-offs
paragraphs: A configurable foundation is not a finished product. The table lists my design choices with the cost each one carries, followed by gaps I can point to in the repository.

The repository holds code from different stages. The backend contains a Config class and a separate pydantic Settings module, and the Dockerfiles and entry-point paths are not uniform across the tree. For this post I re-read the Bot orchestration, memory and anonymizer code and the Compose file; I did not review the route that connects the frontend to the Bot, and I did not run the full stack while writing. Anything that depends on those paths should be checked against a clean run before it is relied on.
There is also no evaluation. I have no benchmark for latency, response quality, anonymization recall or cost, so I report none.

rows: Prompts stay readable to the model and the user sees the original values
A substitution map has to be held and protected; detection is not exhaustive
The chain skips the extra steps when it is disabled
Off in the example file; protection only exists where it is turned on
Retention, deletion and access isolation need explicit decisions

sections.title: What I would do next
paragraphs: My next step is evidence rather than features. I would build a small set of fixed, synthetic conversations and run them while varying the prompt version, the context window and the anonymizer setting. For privacy, I would measure how many seeded identifiers survive into the model input, the stored history and the trace, split by language. For behavior, I would check whether answers stay consistent across the window boundary.

On the engineering side, I would unify the two configuration paths, make the anonymizer flag's wiring explicit and tested, verify per-user isolation of history end to end, and add recognizers for identifiers common in Vietnamese text. Each of these is a plan, not something the repository already does.

takeaways: Keep configuration and orchestration in the backend so that memory, anonymization, the provider and tracing can be changed or debugged independently.
Key history by conversation, and treat retention, deletion and per-user isolation as decisions to make, not defaults.
Reversible anonymization keeps prompts readable, but it is optional here, off in the example file, and not a guarantee of full detection.
Name the steps of the chain so that LangSmith traces show where a request changed; treat the traces themselves as data that needs a policy.
The repository has no benchmarks. Fixed synthetic conversations are the planned way to measure privacy and behavior.
reviewNotes: Confirm which memory class and window size the running backend uses. bot.py defaults to the in-process BASE_MEMORY unless a memory type is passed, and the LangChain Mongo adapter uses a single configured session_id.
Confirm how ENABLE_ANONYMIZER reaches the Bot. common/config.py sets enable_anonymizer to False directly, while backend/config.py (pydantic Settings) reads the environment variable.
The raw tree shows only a /health route in backend/api; confirm which module serves the chat endpoint used by the frontend, and that the Compose stack starts end to end.
The system prompt in the screenshots credits 'Cong Minh and Tran Hieu'. Confirm co-developer credit and which parts you built.
Add a benchmark dataset or measurements before making any accuracy or latency claim.
